job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Chloe Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a car parts supplier outside Nagoya, in the design office. I draw brackets and housings in CAD and update the drawings when the customer changes a hole position. It's detailed, quiet work. I share a small apartment with a friend from university, and I take the train in at 8:10 every morning. I eat the same lunch box at my desk, and I like that the day has a pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. At work I'd carry on with the drawings, and if my section chief mentions new software I'd nod and ask for the manual. I'd tell friends nothing much changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relaxed, honestly. My drawings go to a factory where a human checks them, and the customer's changes keep coming. But I'd still be tense about the car industry, because a bad year at the carmaker hits suppliers like us first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. I'd keep paying into my savings, a little each month, and I'd maybe take the CAD certificate exam, because it looks good. I wouldn't try new tools unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like a steady life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bad year at the carmaker hits you first. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago my firm cut overtime for a full season because orders dropped. My senior colleague Mr Okada said it is how it works, and we all went home at five. It was nice in a way, and also scary, since half the pay was overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about trying new software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm slow, and I know that. I'd rather learn one tool well than five tools badly. If the company gives a course I'll go, but I won't download things at home on my own.

say: Nothing much changes, so I'd carry on with the **drawings**.
If new software appears, I'd nod and ask for the manual.
think: A human checks my drawings at the **factory**, so I feel relaxed.
The real worry is a bad year at the **carmaker** hitting suppliers first.
do: Keep saving a little each month and sit the **CAD certificate** exam.
Avoid new tools unless **the company** requires them.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, though the car industry cycle nags at the back of my mind.
S0.quote: I'd rather learn one tool well than five tools badly.
fieldNote: Her calm hides a **cyclical** pressure: overtime pay at the car supplier is half her income.
She is honest about being slow with new tools.
Her 'steady life' preference is a real value, not a pose.

steps.text: Sit the CAD certificate exam this spring
Put 30,000 yen aside each month for slow overtime seasons
Keep drawing brackets and housings as usual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the drafting software is getting smarter and we'd have to use it. At work I'd say we need training before the machines arrive, not after. My section chief would agree but say budget is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, drawing is the first job at my firm that software can do. The system suggests holes and tolerances, and a design office with five drafters could soon be three. I'd be the newest, so I'd be the first to go, even with good reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to learn the AI features, as much as I hate it, and I'd ask Mr Okada to teach me the judgement part, which tolerances matter. I'd also ask about joining the engineering team that works on prototypes, where it's less drawing and more working with metal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I could lose the one thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the newest drafter goes first. What would you say to your section chief?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm prepared to learn if he shows me the tools, and I'd ask for a seat in the prototype room. He would probably say yes in a polite way and then it would take months. In our company, polite yes can mean wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your life if that went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have savings for about eight months, and my mother in Gifu would feed me if I came home. But I'd feel I'd failed, and I'd not want to say that out loud. I'd look for another design job, maybe at a smaller firm.

say: Drafting software is getting smarter, and we need **training before** the machines arrive.
My section chief would agree but say the budget is tight.
think: Drawing is the **first job** software can do, and as the newest I'd go first.
do: Learn the **AI features** and ask Mr Okada to teach me tolerances.
Ask for a seat in the **prototype room**, closer to real metal.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because I could lose the one thing I'm good at.
S1.quote: In our company, polite yes can mean wait.
fieldNote: She correctly sees her desk as **first in line**.
Her plan hinges on a polite company culture that may not deliver.
Eight months of savings and a home to return to give her a cushion.

steps.text: Ask my section chief to train me on the new CAD features
Ask for a place in the prototype room
Keep eight months of expenses in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too short for a country like ours. I'd tell friends to talk to their families and to keep some cash. At work I'd just keep quiet and wait for the company's announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job would be gone within two years. Drawing is thinking work, and a machine would do it faster and without mistakes. I don't know what I'd do, because I trained for this, and I've never had another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending right away, give up the gym and cook more. I'd go to my parents in Gifu and talk about the future. I'd also look at a vocational course in factory maintenance, because machines still need someone to look after them for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be afraid, to be honest. I'd also feel embarrassed to be afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cook more and give up the gym. What would you cut next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the monthly train to Tokyo to see friends, and I'd share a cheaper apartment, maybe move out of the city. I'd stop buying books and clothes. It sounds small, but I'd feel better if the spending was down before the company said anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why factory maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because robots arrive three years after the thinking machines, and someone has to repair them. It's physical and dull, but my mechanical engineering degree is real. I think I'd be a bit good at it, and it would be a job that exists when others don't.

say: Two years is too short for a country like ours, so friends should **keep some cash**.
At work I'd stay quiet and wait for the company's announcement.
think: My drawing job would be **gone within two years** because it is thinking work.
I trained for this and have never had another job.
do: Cut spending, give up the gym and **cook more**.
Look at a **factory maintenance** course, since someone must repair the robots.
feel: I'd feel **afraid**, and embarrassed to be afraid.
S2.quote: I trained for this, and I've never had another job.
fieldNote: Her job is 100 percent **desk-based**, which is why she goes straight to alarmed.
Strong savings do not stop her imagining a total loss of income.
She chooses maintenance for its link to the hands-on robot delay.

steps.text: Cut spending now by giving up the gym and cooking at home
Visit my parents in Gifu to plan together
Apply for a factory maintenance course for next year
Share a cheaper apartment outside the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a lot better. I'd tell friends to take the time to talk with their families. At work I'd ask if the company can run training about AI and robot maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my drawing job would last a couple of years and then it would change. I'd have time to switch to something related, like production engineering. It's not exciting, but I'd feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to finish my CAD exam, then spend the second year learning about production lines. I'd ask to move to the factory floor for a few months. I'd save more and aim to move to a company that makes machines, not parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious. But I could picture a path, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned moving to a factory floor. What would that give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would let me see what the people on the line actually do. A drafter who has never watched a machine run draws strange things. And on the floor, people notice who is reliable, and I'm reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I must. I would take a course, with a teacher and a clear manual. I don't trust something that I can't see the steps of, but I'd rather be the one in the room who can question it.

say: Five years is better, so I'd ask for **training** on AI and robot maintenance.
I'd tell friends to talk with their families.
think: My drawing job lasts a couple of years, then changes, so I could shift to **production engineering**.
It isn't exciting, but it feels safe.
do: Finish the CAD exam and spend a few months on the **factory floor**.
Aim to join a company that makes **machines**, not parts.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but a clear path helps.
S3.quote: A drafter who has never watched a machine run draws strange things.
fieldNote: A longer clock lets her **move sideways** rather than escape.
She still avoids AI until a proper course exists.
Her reliability is her best asset, and she knows it.

steps.text: Finish my CAD exam in the first year
Ask for three months on the factory floor to learn the production line
Take a company course on AI tools with a teacher

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost normal. I'd say people don't need to panic, but they should learn. I'd tell my friends to keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly okay. By then I'd be 32, and I might be married with a child, or at least in a different job. I'd worry about my parents' retirement more than my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on in my job and use the ten years to build a savings habit. I'd move into production engineering or quality control over time. I'd also help my younger cousin who is studying design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. I'd feel I have time to take small steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about your parents' retirement. What would that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father is a retired machinist and my mother works part time. Their pension is small, and the prices go up every year. If robots and AI make things cheaper that would be fine, but if AI and robots just make companies richer, my parents will still count their yen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the design basics and learn to draw by hand too. I'd say a good eye and a good question will last longer than any program. And I'd say it's okay to be slow, as long as you finish.

say: Ten years feels almost normal, so people shouldn't panic, but they should **keep saving**.
I'd tell friends to learn steadily.
think: By 32 I may be **married with a child**, or in a different job.
I worry more about my **parents' retirement** than my own work.
do: Build a **savings habit** of 40,000 yen a month and drift toward quality control over time.
Help my **cousin** who studies design with drawing basics.
feel: I feel **calm-ish**, because I have time for small steps.
S4.quote: If AI and robots just make companies richer, my parents will still count their yen.
fieldNote: Ten years eases her own fear, but not her **parents' pension** worry.
Her path is a slow slide toward quality control.
She sees herself as a reliable teacher for her cousin.

steps.text: Build a savings habit of 40,000 yen a month
Move toward quality control work over the next decade
Teach my cousin the basics of hand drawing and design

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because I'd have no time to learn another trade. What would help is a clear plan from the government, retraining courses with a real teacher and companies that promise to move drafters into new roles before they let anyone go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I'm not against the new tools. I'm only slow. If someone showed me, step by step, I'd learn, and I think a lot of people feel the same but are too shy to say.

headlineQuote: If someone showed me, step by step, I'd learn, and I think a lot of people feel the same but are too shy to say.
portrait: Chloe is a **22-year-old** mechanical engineer drawing car parts in CAD near Nagoya.
She likes a steady routine, never uses AI tools and moves **slowly** on new software.
Her drawing job is purely desk work, so it is the part of the firm that AI reaches **first**.
She goes from uneasy in a plateau to **alarmed** if AI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries her most, because she'd have no time to learn a new trade.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **government plan**, retraining with a real teacher and promises to move drafters before layoffs.
